meanings.note: Coordinating conjunction pronounced [i] in natural Brazilian speech.

examples.text: Ela faltou e adiantou o trabalho.
examples.trans: She missed it and got ahead on her work.
There are good and bad numbers.

meanings.note: A person being addressed, with third-person verb agreement: você vai, vocês vão. Vai and vão are forms of ir, not forms of the pronoun. Common in Brazil; not a rule that every Brazilian region uses the same address system.

examples.trans: Are you going to the meeting?

meanings.note: Doubled as já, já, it means 'very soon / any minute now'.

examples.trans: Your husband is already doing great.
I have already been in that situation.

meanings.note: Covers knowing facts or finding out information.

examples.text: Eu só quero saber o motivo.
examples.trans: I just want to know the reason.

meanings.note: Definite article agreeing in gender and number with its noun; also common before given names in casual Brazilian speech.

examples.trans: Look at the young woman over there.

meanings.note: All-purpose connector, relative link, question opener, and comparative word after mais or melhor.

examples.text: Eu acho que ele já foi.
examples.trans: I think that he already left.

meanings.note: Vou + infinitive can express a future intention: vou estar means I am going to be. Você takes the third-person vai.
Followed by an infinitive for your own wish (quero saber) or que + subjunctive for someone else (quero que você entre).

examples.text: Eu só quero saber o motivo.
examples.trans: I just want to know the reason.

meanings.note: Expresses sudden realization or understanding.

examples.text: Ah, ele veio fazer implante capilar?
examples.trans: Oh, he came to get a hair implant?

meanings.note: Subject form referring to the speaker. Explicit eu introduces his department in the explanation.
With que it is Brazil's most natural everyday way to say I think / do you think.

examples.text: Eu acho que você tá exagerando.

meanings.note: Indefinite article; plural uns and umas mean some or a few in everyday Brazilian Portuguese.

examples.trans: Shall we have a little coffee?

meanings.note: Romantic or interpersonal bond.
Not heavy or overly serious.

examples.text: Prefiro um jantar leve à noite.
examples.trans: I prefer a light dinner at night.

meanings.note: Relaxed and trouble-free.

examples.text: Quero um relacionamento leve e tranquilo.
examples.trans: I want a light and calm relationship.

meanings.note: Links a meeting with its subject. Do is de + the masculine article o; sou do financeiro identifies membership in the finance department.
Everyday adjective in tá bom (okay), boa tarde (good afternoon), and Bom, pessoal (Well, folks).
Used for identifying a type of meeting or the department a person belongs to. The present forms sou and é are irregular.
Used here for being present at an event. Vou estar keeps estar in the infinitive after the finite form vou.

examples.trans: I’m not going to be at that meeting.
Are you going to be at that meeting?

meanings.note: Covers speaking, talking, and telling in everyday Brazilian speech.

examples.text: Deixa eu te falar uma coisa.

examples.trans: They say a lot of things.

meanings.note: Full form of informal pra; introduces purpose before an infinitive or direction.

examples.trans: I have a lot to sort out.

meanings.note: Regular -er verb.

examples.text: Estou falando de algo para beber e comer.
examples.trans: I am talking about something to drink and eat.
What do you want to drink?.

meanings.note: Regular -er verb.

examples.text: Você já sabe o que quer comer?
examples.trans: Do you already know what you want to eat?
We ate very well at that restaurant.

meanings.en: can; may; to be able to
meanings.note: Core modal verb followed by an infinitive.

examples.text: O senhor pode ser meu fiador?
examples.trans: Can you be my guarantor, sir?

meanings.note: Alcoholic drink made from fermented grapes; vinho tinto is red wine.

examples.trans: It can be red wine, then.

examples.text: Trouxe um vinho bom para nós.
examples.trans: I brought a good wine for us.

meanings.note: Specifically paired with vinho for red wine (vinho tinto).

examples.trans: It can be red wine, then.

examples.text: Pedimos uma taça de vinho tinto.
examples.trans: We ordered a glass of red wine.

meanings.note: Connects a conclusion or agreement.
Used with para/pra for going back to a place.

examples.text: Vou ter que voltar pra casa da minha mãe.
examples.trans: I am going to have to go back to my mother's house.

meanings.note: Used for taking transport, grabbing items, or taking an apartment first.

examples.trans: They will grab it ahead of me.
I do not need to take the subway.

meanings.note: Alone as vocative gente! it means folks/guys; with article a gente it means we/us with third-person singular verbs.

examples.text: Você acha que é melhor que a gente?
examples.trans: Do you think you're better than us?
Oh, folks, the meeting ran late.

meanings.note: Expresses possession, obligation in ter que + infinitive, and impersonal existence (tem alguns números, there are some numbers).

examples.text: Eu tenho que entrar lá dentro.
examples.trans: I have to go inside there.

meanings.note: Used as a quick imperative olha! (look!) and in future subjunctive se vocês olharem (if you look).

examples.text: Se vocês olharem bem, tem números.
examples.trans: If you look closely, there are numbers.

meanings.note: Irregular past trouxe and gerund trazendo.

examples.text: Olha o que eu trouxe para nós.
examples.trans: Look what I brought for us.

examples.text: Esse trabalho está trazendo coisa boa.
examples.trans: This work is bringing good things.

meanings.note: First-person plural pronoun used after prepositions like pra.
Very common Brazilian exclamation expressing surprise, confusion, or pushback.
A negative answer or a negation in a sentence. A final repeated não can reinforce a conversational refusal in Brazil.
Agrees with its noun as a determiner/adjective; singular muita coisa idiomatically means many things.

examples.trans: They say a lot of things.

meanings.note: Taking very little time; also used adverbially.

examples.trans: I will be right back, it is a quick thing.

meanings.note: Polite title; saying sim, senhor to an equal coworker adds mock military obedience.

examples.trans: Are you going in now, sir?

meanings.note: Past participle of atender used as an adjective for a customer who has been waited on.

examples.trans: Have you been helped already, ma'am?

meanings.note: Deixa eu + infinitive is the natural spoken Brazilian frame for let me...

examples.text: Deixa eu te falar uma coisa.

examples.trans: Leave your phone on the desk.

meanings.note: Stands without um for another (outro gráfico), or with os for the others (os outros).
A 24-hour period or a specific date on the calendar.

examples.trans: Let's leave it for another day.

examples.text: Eu nem tenho outro dia livre.
examples.trans: I do not even have another free day.

meanings.note: Comparative and superlative of bom; same singular form for masculine and feminine.

examples.text: Você acha que é melhor que a gente?
examples.trans: Do you think you're better than us?

meanings.note: É verdade means that's true; na verdade means actually; de verdade means really/truly.

examples.trans: That is true, I agree with you.

examples.text: Na verdade, só tenho hoje livre.
examples.trans: Actually, I only have today free.

meanings.note: Very common in spoken Portuguese for loving things, habits, or activities.
